transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2025-10-14 16:00 PT
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Ava Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ruiz (Redwood SE), Priya Shah (NexaHealth Head of Security), Marcus Lee (NexaHealth Cloud Architect), Lena Ortiz (NexaHealth Legal), Tom Bowers (Platform)

[00:00] Ava (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Um, quick round robin?
[00:06] Priya (NexaHealth): Hi, Priya here. We run security for NexaHealth. Looking at Redwood for some inference workloads, we need to nail encryption and key management.
[00:14] Marcus (Cloud Architect): Marcus, I handle the infra side. We'll be testing both hosted and private options.
[00:19] Lena (Legal): Lena from procurement, I'll be taking notes on contractual needs.
[00:23] Ava: Great. Diego, do you want to kick off on how Redwood handles encryption at rest and KMS?
[00:28] Diego (Redwood SE): Sure. So, high level, all data at rest in Redwood is encrypted using envelope encryption. We store data encrypted with a data key, and that data key is itself encrypted with a customer or service master key depending on deployment. For hosted customers we offer Redwood-managed KMS by default, and we support customer-managed keys via AWS KMS, GCP KMS, or Azure Key Vault for BYOK flows.
[00:50] Priya: When you say "support BYOK", does that mean we can import our key material into your environment or you just reference our CMK? We have strict controls, we'd like HSM-backed keys.
[01:02] Diego: Good question. There are two common patterns we discussed: 1) Customer-managed cloud KMS where the CMK is in your cloud project and Redwood is granted limited decrypt/encrypt permissions; 2) Key import where you bring in a key to a supported HSM-backed service. For AWS, for example, we can integrate with a CMK in your account via grants so Redwood never stores plaintext key material. If you want to import a key into a cloud HSM, we can work through the supported import process but there are constraints around key material format and import modes.
[01:34] Marcus: So the usual pattern is envelope encryption and we control the KMS in our AWS account, and Redwood can call our KMS over a secure channel?
[01:42] Diego: Exactly. The runtime will call your KMS for unwrap/rotate operations. We recommend granting an IAM role with narrow permissions and using cross-account grants or conditions like source VPC or mTLS.
[01:53] Priya: What about on-prem HSMs? We run an HSM for our most sensitive keys. Can Redwood call into our HSM or do we need to provision something like CloudHSM or bring a dedicated deployment?
[02:05] Diego: For on-prem HSMs there are two options. One, use Redwood Private (VPC or on-prem package) where the key material and HSM are reachable within your network — Redwood's control plane can be configured to delegate key ops locally. Two, you can use a cloud-hosted HSM (CloudHSM, HSM-backed KMS) and import keys there. Direct calls to a customer-managed on-prem HSM from our hosted control plane are generally constrained by networking and security policies; for that we usually recommend Dedicated or Private deployment so key operations remain inside your network boundary.
[02:40] Marcus: Ok that aligns with our security posture. On rotation — how does key rotation work with BYOK?
[02:47] Diego: We support rotation workflows coordinated with your KMS. If you manage the CMK, you rotate according to your policy and we can re-encrypt data keys during a scheduled maintenance window. If Redwood manages the wrapping key, we rotate based on our cadence but can provide audit logs and rotation records.
[03:02] Priya: Are there any scenarios where Redwood ever has access to plaintext data keys or unencrypted payloads?
[03:08] Diego: Short answer: no for BYOK with CMK in your account. For hosted-managed keys we use strict controls — keys are in HSM-backed services and access is controlled by KMS policies, and we avoid persisting plaintext. During runtime there are ephemeral decrypted keys in memory within the serving instances, but we don't persist them.
[03:26] Tom (Platform): Are the runtime instances inside the same VPC as the KMS calls? How do you ensure network-level access restrictions?
[03:33] Diego: For Dedicated/Private the instances can be in your VPC or peered VPCs; we support VPC peering and private connectivity. For hosted, we recommend the cross-account grant + condition that limits key use to specific source IP ranges or TLS client certs. We also support mTLS for private endpoints when doing KMS calls in environments that support it.
[03:54] Priya: Audit logs — we need proof of key usage and access. What logs do we get?
[04:00] Diego: We surface audit logs in two places: the cloud KMS logs (e.g., CloudTrail for AWS KMS) which show key usage events, and Redwood's operational logs which include token-level access, model route, request metadata, and KMS call correlation IDs. We can push those logs to your logging backends or provide S3/secure storage exports.
[04:19] Priya: Retention and tamper evidence? We need logs retained for a year and to show tamper-evidence for audits.
[04:26] Ava: We have configurable log retention in Dedicated/Private, and for hosted customers we offer enterprise retention add-ons. Redwood signs some audit artifacts and we can provide EVIDs for critical events; Diego can follow up with the exact retention SLAs and export formats.
[04:39] Lena: From a legal perspective, any contract clauses we should be aware of re: key ownership? We need explicit text that customer retains ownership of keys and that Redwood will not export keys.
[04:49] Ava: Yes, we have standard BYOK clauses that state customer retains key ownership and Redwood acts as a crypto-op agent when granted. We'll share the template as part of the procurement packet.
[04:57] Marcus: Is there support for HSM-backed signing for attestations or key derivation? We use a signing key in HSM for some audit flows.
[05:05] Diego: We can support HSM-backed operations when the HSM is in your control or in a supported cloud HSM. For signing we usually recommend doing the signing inside your KMS/HSM and passing us signatures or attestation artifacts. If you need Redwood to produce signed audit artifacts, we have options via customer-managed key stores or via a Redwood attestation key with limited use; that'll need legal/POC discussion.
[05:28] Priya: Data residency — we have EU patient data; can you ensure data never leaves eu-west-1?
[05:35] Ava: Yes, Redwood supports region pinning for hosted and we can do Private/VPC for strict residency. For hosted we can route requests and maintain storage in the chosen region. We'll need to confirm model availability in that region.
[05:47] Marcus: Any perf impact when using BYOK with cross-account KMS calls? We care about latency as these are low-latency inference calls.
[05:55] Diego: There is a small latency hit during initial unwrap/rotate or when cache misses occur. We do prefix/KV caching so we avoid KMS per-token calls — typically KMS is used to unwrap data keys at session start or when keys rotate, not per inference token. For high-throughput we recommend Dedicated with local key caches and smaller unwrapping frequency. We'll share benchmarks with encrypted workloads.
[06:20] Priya: What about key lifecycle — backup, export, destroy?
[06:25] Diego: Backup/export depends on KMS. If you manage keys in your account, backup/export is governed by your KMS/HSM policy. If you import keys into a cloud HSM, import and export are limited by the HSM vendor; often export is disallowed for certain key types. Destruction can be done via KMS schedule or manual destroy and we can coordinate for compliance.
[06:45] Priya: Can you do FIPS validated crypto? Our procurement requires FIPS 140-2 validated modules for certain operations.
[06:52] Diego: Our cloud integrations use HSM-backed services that are FIPS-compliant where available (e.g., AWS KMS with FIPS endpoints). For Private/on-prem we can certify the HSMs you choose. We'll confirm specific module compliance in the follow-up.
[07:05] Tom: Is data encrypted at rest in ephemeral cache layers and local SSDs on the serving nodes?
[07:10] Diego: Yes, ephemeral caches and local storage are encrypted. We use encrypted disks and we avoid persisting plaintext beyond memory. If using Dedicated, the storage is provisioned within your environment with your encryption controls where applicable.
[07:23] Priya: A couple of smaller items — how do you handle key compromise? Revocation and re-keying?
[07:29] Diego: We have an incident playbook: immediate revoke/grant removal, rotate CMKs, re-encrypt data keys, and run a forensic export of access logs. We'll provide our incident response summary doc; action item for Ava to send it.
[07:42] Ava: Yep, I'll send the incident response summary along with SOC2 artifacts.
[07:46] Marcus: Any limitations on the algorithms supported? We need AES-GCM, RSA for signing, and ECC for some flows.
[07:52] Diego: We support industry-standard algorithms via the KMS providers — AES-GCM for data keys and RSA/ECC for signing depending on the KMS/HSM. If you have a specific curve/version requirement, let us know.
[08:03] Priya: Ok, last thing — can we run a short PoC where we provision a customer-managed CMK and run a set of inference jobs to see latency and log outputs?
[08:12] Ava: Absolutely. Typical PoC is 2-4 weeks: Redwood provides a dedicated/GW endpoint or Private instance, we run a throughput and latency benchmark with your sample dataset. We'll instrument KMS calls and provide logs.
[08:24] Lena: For procurement we'll need pricing for Dedicated with BYOK, and any fees for HSM operations.
[08:29] Ava: We'll include that in the follow-up pricing packet.
[08:33] Diego: I'll also include the HSM import constraints doc so you can see what's allowed and what's not for each vendor.
[08:40] Priya: Great. Thanks everyone.
[08:43] Ava: Recap / next steps — I'll share SOC2, ISO summary, incident playbook, and whitepaper; Diego will schedule HSM deep-dive and send architecture diagrams; Marcus will provide sample data and VPC details; Lena will confirm procurement timeline.
[08:58] Ava: Any other questions?
[09:01] Marcus: None from me.
[09:03] Priya: All good. Thanks.
[09:05] Ava: Thanks all. We'll follow up by end of week.
